---
title: "The Journey"
subtitle: "Three attempts to teach a computer to read handwriting."
---

This project did not start with the solution it uses today. It went through
three distinct attempts, each one a response to the limitations of the technology
available at the time and a reflection of a steep personal learning curve.

It would be inaccurate to view these methods as competing options; rather,
they represent an evolution over time. When this work began, a site-specific
custom pipeline was the only programmatic alternative to manually typing out
data from all 12,000 cards one by one. Each subsequent iteration benefited from
rapid advancements in machine learning frameworks and an increasing familiarity
with modern coding tools.

## Attempt 1: Building a custom pipeline from scratch

The first idea was the most intuitive one. If a computer needs to read specific
handwriting on specific forms, you build and train a system from scratch to do
exactly that.

Using classic data science libraries like **scikit-learn** and deep learning
frameworks like **PyTorch**, this approach required manually segmenting images
and painstakingly labeling training data character by character, line by line.
The goal was to feed thousands of exact examples into a custom architecture so
it could learn to map images of text to the actual characters they represented.

The bottleneck here was **variation** paired with the sheer scale of manual labor
required for a single person working in their spare time. The archive spans over
fifty years and contains the handwriting of dozens of different staff members.
Some entries are in typewriter text, others in crisp pen, still others are written
in faint pencil, and a few are ghostly carbon copies.

To make a custom PyTorch model robust enough to handle this level of noise,
it required an impractical amount of manually labeled training data.
Without it, the model simply could not generalize across different eras
and handwriting styles.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What this taught me.** Custom training works beautifully when data is
completely uniform. When data is historical, messy, and varied, you waste months
labeling data just to get a model to recognize basic shapes. To avoid this, you need
a model that already arrives with a general understanding of what writing looks like.
:::

## Attempt 2: OpenCV alignment and Google Cloud Vision

The second approach split the problem in two: use computer vision to find
things on the card, and use a commercial cloud service to read them.

The first half worked beautifully. Using **OpenCV**, a widely used open-source
computer vision library, I built an image alignment module that could reliably
locate the card within a scanned page. A multi-template matching approach
tried several anchor variations to find the best alignment, achieving 100%
success on card detection.

The plan was to combine this geometric alignment with fixed-coordinate
templates: if the card is aligned, then the species name is always at these
pixel coordinates, the accession number is always at those coordinates, and so
on. But propagation cards are not standardized forms. Propagators wrote outside
boxes, used margins for notes, and the internal layout shifted across decades.
Fixed coordinates broke immediately.

The pivot was to use **Google Cloud Vision** for the reading itself. Google's
API returned both the recognized text and the pixel coordinates of each word
on the page. Custom code then mapped those word positions back to structured
fields based on proximity to known field labels: a form of dynamic template
matching that adapted to wherever the text actually appeared.

This strategy yielded highly readable text outputs. The cloud engine handled
handwriting variations with ease because it was built upon the exact deep-learning
principles experimented with in Attempt 1, but scaled across billions of data points.
On the fields it targeted, the approach reached roughly 90 to 98 percent accuracy.

However, the approach was ultimately abandoned due to institutional reality.
Processing thousands of records would have meant sending sensitive institutional
collection data, including wild-collection provenance and donor details, to external
corporate servers. It became clear that navigating data sovereignty and securing
institutional approval for off-site processing was a massive hurdle.
Furthermore, template matching, even the dynamic version, proved exceptionally brittle.
The moment a horticulturist built a condensed propagation table or reused the back
of a card for a different species, the spatial logic broke entirely.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What this taught me.** General-purpose models solve the handwriting barrier,
but cloud dependencies introduce issues with data sovereignty, subscription fees,
and corporate reliance. For an institution prioritizing data privacy and
long-term autonomy, cloud-only pipelines are frequently a non-starter.
:::

## Attempt 3: Local vision language models

The current iteration of this project is cutting-edge, utilizing tools and
architectures that did not exist even a year ago. The convergence of open-weight
vision models, local execution engines like **Ollama**, local computing nodes,
and advanced agentic development tools over the past 12 months has fundamentally
changed what is possible on ordinary hardware. I say this not as a boast but as a
call to regular folks like myself: these techniques are now available to the masses.

Instead of traditional OCR that looks at characters in isolation, a
**Vision Language Model (VLM)** views the entire image holistically. It reads a
propagation card much like a human archivist would: interpreting terms from context,
parsing layout structure naturally, and outputting clean text.

### Finding the right model

The development of this pipeline began on a small desktop node running
**Gemma 3**, Google's open-weight model, served locally through Ollama. Gemma
handled general text well, but its accuracy on the specific challenges of
propagation cards, faded handwriting, botanical Latin, and condensed tables,
was not sufficient for production use.

When the pipeline moved to a MacBook for deployment, **Qwen 2.5-VL** had just
been released by Alibaba's research team. The Qwen family offered
vision-language models at several sizes, and initial testing showed markedly
better performance on handwritten botanical records.

The question became which size to use. Larger models (12B and 14B parameters)
produced slightly better transcriptions, but combining their memory footprint
with the high-DPI scans required to read faded writing quickly overwhelmed the
machine's 24 GB of unified RAM. The model and the image compete for the same
memory: a larger model means less room for a detailed scan, and vice versa.

**Qwen 2.5-VL at 7 billion parameters, paired with 175 DPI scans**, struck
the balance. The model was sharp enough to read decades of varied handwriting,
and the scan resolution was high enough to preserve faded characters, all
within the memory budget of a single laptop. This is the configuration that
processed the full archive.

It is worth noting that there is no strict adherence to this specific model.
Other botanical gardens adapting this tool should absolutely experiment with
newer, larger models if they have the hardware to support them. I designed
this as a "one and done" solution; the results are good enough that I expect
never to have to run this archive again.

### The virtue of patience

Running a multi-billion-parameter neural network locally on a desktop or a repurposed
hardware node changes the performance dynamic. It is slower than a massive cloud
data center.

However, as horticulturists, we are intimately familiar with waiting.
When you sow a seed, you don't expect results overnight; we understand that complex
systems take time to yield results. Local machine learning requires a similar mindset.
The trade-off for absolute data sovereignty and zero operational cost is processing time.
We are perfectly comfortable letting a local machine quietly run through the night,
germinating structured data from cold pixels at its own steady pace.

### Splitting the labor

To maximize accuracy on local hardware, the codebase splits the work into
a two-part pipeline:

1. **The model reads.** The VLM is instructed strictly to transcribe everything
it sees as a faithful observer. It is not asked to format or interpret data during
the vision pass, which preserves its full cognitive capacity for raw comprehension.
2. **The code checks.** A robust post-processing layer handles the rigid logic:
formatting dates, isolating accession strings, and executing
**Retrieval-Augmented Validation (RAV)** against internal collection reports to
catch spelling errors or typos.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What this taught me.** You do not need to build your own AI from scratch,
nor do you need to pay for massive cloud infrastructure. A compact, open-weight model
running locally can handle historical records beautifully if you divide the labor.
Let the model do the probabilistic reading and let deterministic local code handle
the structural verification.
:::

## The technological arc

Looking back across the entire development process reveals how the underlying
paradigm has shifted:

| Feature | Attempt 1 | Attempt 2 | Attempt 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Core Approach** | Custom PyTorch Pipeline | OpenCV Alignment + Cloud API | Local Vision Language Model |
| **Data Privacy** | Local, but labor-intensive | Cloud-dependent (data leaves site) | Absolute (runs completely offline) |
| **Layout Adaptability** | Rigid | Brittle (fails on non-standard layouts) | Holistic (understands complex layouts) |
| **Cost Structure** | High cost in manual labeling time | Recurring per-image API fees | Free (amortized hardware + electricity) |
| **Model Progression** | N/A | Google Cloud Vision | Gemma 3 then Qwen 2.5-VL 7B |
| **Development Feasibility** | Required deep developer expertise | Required cloud infrastructure setup | Accelerated by modern local tools |

The evolution of this project mirrors a broader democratization of technology.
The tools did not simply get more accurate; they became accessible enough
for an environmental professional to build, deploy, and control locally within
a nursery setting.
